title: Blue Square in Hannam-dong: Seoul's Favorite Musical Theater, Concert Hall, and Book Café (Beginner's Guide)
html:
If you're spending an evening in Seoul and want to see a musical, hear a concert, or just hide out in a quiet, beautiful bookstore for a few hours, there's a good chance you'll end up at Blue Square. It's a big culture complex in Hannam-dong, right next to Itaewon, and it's one of the easiest "real Korean nightlife" spots for first-time visitors to try, since almost everything about it — tickets, signage, directions — is simple to figure out even if you don't speak Korean. Here's what it actually is, what's inside, and how to visit it without any confusion.

What Exactly Is Blue Square?

Photo: Blue Square exterior, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

Blue Square is a multi-purpose culture building that opened in 2011 in Hannam-dong, Yongsan-gu — the same neighborhood as Itaewon, just a short walk from the busier main street. Inside one building, it combines a large musical theater, a concert hall, a bookstore café, and a rooftop café with a view of Namsan Mountain. If you've never been to Korea before, think of it as something between a Broadway theater and a bookshop-café hybrid, all under one roof — a very "Seoul" way to spend a few hours.

The building is spread over four floors above ground and four below (B4–4F), so it's bigger inside than it looks from the street. You don't need a ticket to just walk in and look around, grab a coffee, or browse the bookstore — only the performances themselves require tickets.

The Two Main Halls: Musicals and Concerts

Photo: Blue Square lobby area, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

Blue Square has two main performance spaces, and in Korea it's common for companies to pay for "naming rights," so the hall names you see on tickets and signs are sponsor names, not the venue's own name:

  • Shinhan Card Hall — the dedicated musical theater, seating around 1,700 people. This is where most of the big-name musicals Seoul is known for (Korean-language productions of Western hits, plus original Korean musicals) run for weeks or months at a time.
  • Mastercard Hall — a multi-purpose concert hall seating around 1,400, used for K-pop and other concerts, fan meetings, and other live shows.

Because these are sponsor names, don't be surprised if you see the venue referred to by a slightly different hall name in an older blog post or guidebook — Koreans themselves just say "Blue Square" and figure out the hall from the ticket. Tickets for most shows are sold through Interpark Ticket (also available in English on their app/website), and popular musicals and K-pop-adjacent concerts can sell out fast, so it's worth booking a few weeks ahead if you already know the dates of your trip.

Book Park: The Café Every Local Recommends

Photo: Interior of Blue Square's book café area, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

Even if you have no interest in a musical or a concert, Blue Square is worth visiting just for Book Park, a large reading lounge and café on the 3rd floor with close to 3,000 carefully chosen books (a good number of them in English, alongside Korean titles). It works a bit differently from a normal café: you pay one entry fee to sit as long as you like and read, rather than paying per drink.

  • Hours: roughly 11:30–21:00, last order 19:00. Closed on Mondays.
  • Price: around 12,900 KRW on weekdays for the full day; weekends and holidays are priced by time block (2 hrs / 4 hrs / 6 hrs). A coffee or tea is included in the entry fee.
  • Same-day musical or concert ticket holders usually get a small discount, so keep your ticket on hand.

This is exactly the kind of "quiet escape from the city" that plenty of Koreans themselves go out of their way for — it's less of a tourist spot and more of a genuine local favorite for a slow afternoon. If you'd rather sit outside, there's also a rooftop café called Pilos with a terrace view toward Namsan Mountain, on the opposite end of the building from Book Park.

Getting There and Practical Info

Photo: Street-level view near Blue Square, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

Blue Square sits right next to Hangangjin Station (Line 6), so it's an easy subway trip from most parts of Seoul — you can walk straight there from the station without needing a taxi. The full address is 294 Itaewon-ro, Yongsan-gu, Seoul (한남동).

  • Parking: available on-site; roughly 5,000 KRW for the first 4 hours for performance ticket holders, then about 1,000 KRW per 10 minutes after that. If you're not driving, the subway is simpler.
  • Opening hours for shows: there's no single "opening time" — each hall operates around its own performance schedule, so always check the specific show's start time on Interpark Ticket rather than assuming a fixed schedule.
  • Nearby: since you're already at the edge of Itaewon, it's easy to combine a Blue Square visit with dinner or a walk around Itaewon's restaurant streets before or after a show.

Tips for First-Time Visitors

Photo: Blue Square building view, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

  • Book tickets on Interpark Ticket's English site/app ahead of time rather than hoping to buy at the door — big musicals and concerts frequently sell out, especially on weekends.
  • Musicals here are performed in Korean even when the story is a famous Western one (like a Korean-language production of a Broadway hit). Some productions offer English subtitles on a side screen for certain showings — check the specific listing on Interpark before buying if that matters to you.
  • Arrive 20–30 minutes early if you want time to look around the lobby, use the restroom, or grab a quick drink — lobbies can get crowded right before showtime.
  • If you just want the café, go on a weekday afternoon when it's quieter, and bring a book or laptop — Book Park is genuinely set up for sitting a while, not a quick coffee stop.

💬 Planning a show at Blue Square, or just curious about the Book Park café? Drop your question in the comments below — happy to help!
